slides.title: The problem and its setting
slides.lead: A linear map can do several things at once.
body: It can stretch some vectors, shrink others, rotate directions, or send a space into a higher-dimensional one. Sometimes it sends a nonzero vector to zero. What if we want to separate the information about length change from everything else? For a real number a, its absolute value tells us how much multiplication by a changes length. Multiplying by negative three reverses a direction and triples its length; the absolute value, three, remembers only the length change. There is an operator construction with the same purpose.

slides.title: Start with the length of an output
slides.lead: Let A map one finite-dimensional inner-product space E into another space F.
body: The two spaces do not have to have the same dimension. Choose a vector x in E. We know that the squared length of A x is the inner product of A x with itself. By the defining identity of the adjoint, this is also the inner product of x with A adjoint A x. So the squared output length is determined entirely by the source Gram operator, A adjoint A. That is an important observation. The expression A adjoint A acts on the input space E, even though A x lives in the output space F. This lets us measure the stretching without moving into the output space.

slides.title: Why the modulus preserves the output lengths
slides.lead: Call the modulus M for a moment.
body: Since M is positive, it is self-adjoint. And by construction, M squared is A adjoint A. Now compute the squared length of M x. Using the adjoint identity, this equals the inner product of x with M adjoint M x. But M adjoint is M, so M adjoint M is M squared, which is A adjoint A. We are back to the squared length of A x. Thus M x and A x always have the same length. In spoken terms: the modulus of A stretches every input vector by exactly the same amount as A does. This does not mean they produce the same output vector. They may not even live in the same space. A x lies in F, while M x lies in E.

slides.title: A two-dimensional example
slides.lead: Let A take the vector with coordinates x and y and output the vector whose first coordinate is x plus y and whose second coordinate is zero.
body: The matrix of A has first row one, one and second row zero, zero. What happens to lengths? The output has length equal to the absolute value of x plus y. The input direction with equal coordinates survives and gets stretched. The direction with opposite coordinates disappears completely. Compute A adjoint A. Because we are using real coordinates, adjoint means transpose. The result is the two-by-two matrix with every entry equal to one.

slides.title: Three examples that test the definition
slides.lead: First, suppose A is itself a positive operator on E.
body: It is already the unique positive square root of A squared. Because A adjoint equals A, the modulus of A equals A. A positive operator has no sign or orientation change for the modulus to remove. Second, suppose A is a unitary operator, or more generally an isometric embedding. Every input length is preserved. The defining adjoint identity for an isometry is A adjoint A equals the identity on E. The positive square root of the identity is the identity. Therefore the modulus of any isometry is simply the identity on its input space. Third, suppose A is self-adjoint but has both positive and negative eigenvalues.

slides.title: Kernels and directions that disappear
slides.lead: We can now prove a useful kernel identity.
body: If A kills x, its output length is zero. The modulus produces an output of exactly the same length, so the modulus also kills x. Conversely, if the modulus kills x, the output length of A x must also be zero. Thus A kills x. So A and its modulus have precisely the same kernel. The kernel marks the input directions that disappear. The orthogonal complement of the kernel consists of directions on which there is no complete collapse. Later, the partial isometry in the polar decomposition will preserve lengths on that orthogonal complement and vanish on the kernel. Notice that none of this required A to be invertible.

slides.title: Modulus and the operator norm
slides.lead: Recall that the operator norm of A is the largest output length among inputs of length one.
body: Because A and its modulus produce equal lengths on every input, their operator norms are equal. The modulus has an extra advantage: it is positive and self-adjoint, so the finite spectral theorem applies. Its operator norm is its largest eigenvalue. Consequently, the largest possible stretching factor of A can be found by inspecting the eigenvalues of its modulus. The complete ordered list of these nonnegative eigenvalues will become the singular values of A. So singular values are not mysterious numbers attached to an arbitrary rectangular matrix.

slides.title: What we have and what is still missing
slides.lead: We now know how to construct a canonical positive operator that captures the lengths produced by A.
body: We know its square, its kernel, and its largest eigenvalue interpretation. What we do not yet know is how to match each input stretching direction with its corresponding direction in the output space. That relationship is what singular-value decomposition will provide. Try to reconstruct the chain before moving on: squared length of A x, then the Gram operator A adjoint A, then the positive square root, then equality of output lengths. Explain why the modulus lives on the source space even for a rectangular map. And check the example where A maps x and y to x plus y and zero.
